n:
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “anointed,” i.e., designated to carry out an assigned task.

*Study note:* The speaker is not identified, but he is distinct from the Lord and from Zion’s suffering people. He possesses the divine spirit, is God’s spokesman, and is sent to release prisoners from bondage. The evidence suggests he is the Lord’s special servant, described earlier in the servant songs (see {{Isaiah 42:1|42:1-4}}, {{Isaiah 42:7|7}}; {{Isaiah 49:2|49:2}}, {{Isaiah 49:9|9}}; {{Isaiah 50:4|50:4}}; see also {{Isaiah 51:16|51:16}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “sent” (NAB); NCV “has appointed me.”

*Translator's note:* Or “proclaim good news to.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to bind up [the wounds of].”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to announce the year of the Lord’s favor, and the day of our God’s vengeance.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “oil of joy” (KJV, ASV, NIV11); NASB, NIV84, NRSV “the oil of gladness.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “garment of praise.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a faint spirit” (so NRSV); KJV, ASV “the spirit of heaviness”; NASB “a spirit of fainting.”

*Translator's note:* Rather than referring to the character of the people, צֶדֶק (tsedeq) may carry the nuance “vindication” here, suggesting that God’s restored people are a testimony to his justice. See v. {{Isaiah 61:2|2}}, which alludes to the fact that God will take vengeance against the enemies of his people. Cf. NAB “oaks of justice.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a planting of the Lord to reveal splendor.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the formerly desolate places they will raise up.”

*Study note:* The Lord speaks in vv. {{Isaiah 61:7|7-8}} (and possibly v. {{Isaiah 61:9|9}}). It is not clear where the servant’s speech (see vv. {{Isaiah 61:1|1-3a}}) ends and the Lord’s begins. Perhaps the direct address to the people signals the beginning of the Lord’s speech.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will stand [in position] and shepherd.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text adds, “it will be said concerning you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “eat” (KJV, NAB, NASB); NIV “feed on”; NLT “be fed with.”

*Text-critical note:* The form in the Hebrew text probably needs to be emended to יִתְאַמְּרוּ (yitʾammeru), a Hitpael from אָמַר (ʾamar), meaning “boast about” (see *HALOT* 67 s.v. II אמר, *HALOT* 416 s.v. ימר, and BDB 56 s.v. אָמַר).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “their glory” (i.e., riches).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “instead of your shame, a double portion.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and [instead of] humiliation they will rejoice [over] their portion.” The term תַחַת (takhat, “instead of”) is understood by ellipsis (note the preceding line).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “therefore” (so KJV, NASB); NIV “and so.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all who see them will recognize them, that they [are] descendants [whom] the Lord has blessed.”

*Study note:* The speaker in vv. {{Isaiah 61:10|10-11}} is not identified, but it is likely that the personified nation (or perhaps Zion) responds here to the Lord’s promise of restoration.

*Translator's note:* The infinitive absolute appears before the finite verb for emphasis.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my being is happy in my God”; NAB “in my God is the joy of my soul.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “robe of vindication”; KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV “robe of righteousness.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like a bridegroom [who] acts like a priest [by wearing] a turban, and like a bride [who] wears her jewelry.” The words “I look” are supplied for stylistic reasons and clarification.

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps, “righteousness,” but the context seems to emphasize deliverance and restoration (see v. {{Isaiah 61:10|10}} and {{Isaiah 62:1|62:1}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and praise before all the nations.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “which the mouth of the Lord will designate.”

*Translator's note:* Or “for”; KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV “but.”

*Translator's note:* Hebrew חֶפְצִי־בָהּ (kheftsi vah), traditionally transliterated “Hephzibah” (so KJV, ASV, NIV).

*Translator's note:* Hebrew בְּעוּלָה (beʿulah), traditionally transliterated “Beulah” (so KJV, ASV, NIV).

*Translator's note:* That is, the land will be restored to the Lord’s favor and once again enjoy his blessing and protection. To indicate the land’s relationship to the Lord, the words “to him” have been supplied at the end of the clause.

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text has “your sons,” but this produces an odd metaphor and is somewhat incongruous with the parallelism. In the context (v. {{Isaiah 62:4|4b}}, see also {{Isaiah 54:5|54:5-7}}) the Lord is the one who “marries” Zion. Therefore several prefer to emend “your sons” to בֹּנָיִךְ (bonayikh, “your builder”; e.g., NRSV). In {{Psalm 147:2|Ps 147:2}} the Lord is called the “builder of Jerusalem.” However, this emendation is not the best option for at least four reasons. First, although the Lord is never called the “builder” of Jerusalem in Isaiah, the idea of Zion’s children possessing the land does occur ({{Isaiah 49:20|Isa 49:20}}; {{Isaiah 54:3|54:3}}; cf. also {{Isaiah 14:1|14:1}}; {{Isaiah 60:21|60:21}}). Secondly, all the ancient versions support the MT reading. Thirdly, although the verb בָּעַל (baʿal) can mean “to marry,” its basic idea is “to possess.” Consequently, the verb stresses a relationship more than a state. All the ancient versions render this verb “to dwell in” or “to dwell with.” The point is not just that the land will be reinhabited, but that it will be in a relationship of “belonging” to the Israelites. Hence a relational verb like בָּעַל is used (J. N. Oswalt, *Isaiah* [NICOT], 2:581). Finally, “sons” is a well-known metaphor for “inhabitants” (J. de Waard, *Isaiah*, 208).

*Study note:* The speaker here is probably the prophet.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all day and all night continually they do not keep silent.” The following lines suggest that they pray for the Lord’s intervention and restoration of the city.

*Translator's note:* Or “invoke”; NIV “call on”; NASB, NRSV “remind.”

*Translator's note:* “Jerusalem” is supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons; note the following line.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[the object of] praise.”
*Translator's note:* The Lord’s right hand and strong arm here symbolize his power and remind the audience that his might guarantees the fulfillment of the following promise.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it,” the grain mentioned in v. {{Isaiah 62:8|8a}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and those who gather it will drink it.” The masculine singular pronominal suffixes attached to “gather” and “drink” refer back to the masculine noun תִּירוֹשׁ (tirosh, “wine”) in v. {{Isaiah 62:8|8b}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to the end of the earth” (so NASB, NRSV).

*Study note:* As v. {{Isaiah 62:12|12}} indicates, the returning exiles are the Lord’s reward/prize. See also {{Isaiah 40:10|40:10}} and the note there.
*Translator's note:* Or “the redeemed of the Lord” (KJV, NAB).

*Study note:* Edom is here an archetype for the Lord’s enemies. See {{Isaiah 34:5|34:5}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[in] bright red garments, from Bozrah.”

*Translator's note:* The interrogative particle is understood by ellipsis; note the first line of the verse.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “honored in his clothing”; KJV, ASV “glorious in his apparel.”

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text has צָעָה (tsaʿah), which means “stoop, bend” ({{Isaiah 51:14|51:14}}). The translation assumes an emendation to צָעַד (tsaʿad, “march”; see BDB 858 s.v. צָעָה).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I, [the one] speaking in vindication [or “righteousness”], great to deliver.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and your garments like one who treads in a vat?”

*Study note:* Nations, headed by Edom, are the object of the Lord’s anger (see v. {{Isaiah 63:6|6}}). He compares military slaughter to stomping on grapes in a vat.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and I stained.” For discussion of the difficult verb form, see *HALOT* 170 s.v. II גאל. Perhaps the form is mixed, combining the first person forms of the imperfect (note the alef prefix) and perfect (note the תי- ending).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for the day of vengeance was in my heart, and the year of my revenge came.” The term גְּאוּלַי (geʾulay) is sometimes translated here “my redemption,” for the verbal root גאל often means “deliver, buy back.” A גֹּאֵל (goʾel, “kinsman-redeemer”) was responsible for protecting the extended family’s interests, often by redeeming property that had been sold outside the family. However, the responsibilities of a גֹּאֵל extended beyond financial concerns. He was also responsible for avenging the shed blood of a family member (see {{Numbers 35:19|Num 35:19-27}}; {{Deuteronomy 19:6|Deut 19:6-12}}). In {{Isaiah 63:4|Isa 63:4}}, where vengeance is a prominent theme (note the previous line), it is probably this function of the family protector that is in view. The Lord pictures himself as a blood avenger who waits for the day of vengeance to arrive and then springs into action.

*Study note:* See {{Isaiah 59:16|Isa 59:16}} for similar language.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and my anger, it supported me”; NIV “my own wrath sustained me.”

*Study note:* See {{Isaiah 49:26|Isa 49:26}} and {{Isaiah 51:23|51:23}} for similar imagery.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and I brought down to the ground their juice.” “Juice” refers to their blood (see v. {{Isaiah 63:3|3}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “according to all which.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “greatness of goodness to the house of Israel which he did for them.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “according to.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “children [who] do not act deceitfully.” Here the verb refers to covenantal loyalty.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in all their distress, there was distress to him” (reading לוֹ [lo] with the margin/*Qere*).

*Study note:* This may refer to the “angel of God” mentioned in {{Exodus 14:19|Exod 14:19}}, who in turn may be identical to the divine “presence” (literally, “face”) referred to in {{Exodus 33:14|Exod 33:14-15}} and {{Deuteronomy 4:37|Deut 4:37}}. Here in {{Isaiah 63|Isa 63}} this messenger may be equated with God’s “holy Spirit” (see vv. {{Isaiah 63:10|10-11}}) and “the Spirit of the Lord” (v. {{Isaiah 63:14|14}}). See also {{Psalm 139:7|Ps 139:7}}, where God’s “Spirit” seems to be equated with his “presence” (literally, “face”) in the synonymous parallelistic structure.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the messenger [or “angel”] of his face”; NIV “the angel of his presence.”

*Translator's note:* Or “redeemed” (KJV, NAB, NIV), or “delivered.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all the days of antiquity”; KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV “days of old.”

*Translator's note:* Or “grieved, hurt the feelings of.”

*Study note:* The phrase “Holy Spirit” occurs in the OT only here (in v. {{Isaiah 63:11|11}} as well) and in {{Psalm 51:11|Ps 51:11}} (51:13 HT), where it is associated with the divine presence.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he remembered the days of antiquity, Moses, his people.” The syntax of the statement is unclear. The translation assumes that “his people” is the subject of the verb “remembered.” If original, “Moses” is in apposition to “the days of antiquity,” more precisely identifying the time period referred to. However, the syntactical awkwardness suggests that “Moses” may have been an early marginal note (perhaps identifying “the shepherd of his flock” two lines later) that has worked its way into the text.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has a plural form, which if retained and taken as a numerical plural, would probably refer to Moses, Aaron, and the Israelite tribal leaders at the time of the Exodus. Most prefer to emend the form to the singular (רָעָה, raʿah) and understand this as a reference just to Moses.

*Study note:* See the note at v. {{Isaiah 63:10|10}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who caused to go at the right hand of Moses the arm of his splendor.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “making for himself a lasting name.”

*Translator's note:* The words “to graze” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* Or “so” (KJV, ASV), or “thus” (NAB, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “making for yourself a majestic name.”

*Translator's note:* This probably refers to his zeal for his people, which motivates him to angrily strike out against their enemies.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text reads literally, “the agitation of your intestines and your compassion to me they are held back.” The phrase “agitation of your intestines” is metonymic, referring to the way in which one’s nervous system reacts when one feels pity and compassion toward another. אֵלַי (ʾelay, “to me”) is awkward in this context, where the speaker represents the nation and, following the introduction (see v. {{Isaiah 63:7|7}}), utilizes first person plural forms. The translation assumes an emendation to the negative particle אַל (ʾal). This also necessitates emending the following verb form (which is a plural perfect) to a singular jussive (תִתְאַפָּק, titʾappaq). The Hitpael of אָפַק (ʾafaq) also occurs in {{Isaiah 42:14|42:14}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “our protector [or “redeemer”] from antiquity [is] your name.”

*Translator's note:* Some suggest a tolerative use of the Hiphil here, “[why do] you allow us to stray?” (cf. NLT). Though the Hiphil of תָעָה (taʿah) appears to be tolerative in Jer 50:6, elsewhere it is preferable or necessary to take it as causative. See {{Isaiah 3:12|Isa 3:12}}; {{Isaiah 9:15|9:15}}; and {{Isaiah 30:28|30:28}}, as well as {{Genesis 20:13|Gen 20:13}}; {{2 Kings 21:9|2 Kgs 21:9}}; {{Job 12:24|Job 12:24-25}}; {{Proverbs 12:26|Prov 12:26}}; Jer 23:13, 32; Hos 4:12; {{Amos 2:4|Amos 2:4}}; {{Micah 3:5|Mic 3:5}}.

*Translator's note:* This probably refers to God’s commands.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[Why do] you harden our heart[s] so as not to fear you.” The interrogative particle is understood by ellipsis (note the preceding line).

*Study note:* How direct this hardening is, one cannot be sure. The speaker may envision direct involvement on the Lord’s part. The Lord has brought the exile as judgment for the nation’s sin and now he continues to keep them at arm’s length by blinding them spiritually. The second half of {{Isaiah 64:7|64:7}} might support this, though the precise reading of the final verb is uncertain. On the other hand, the idiom of lament is sometimes ironic and hyperbolically deterministic. For example, Naomi lamented that Shaddai was directly opposing her and bringing her calamity ({{Ruth 1:20|Ruth 1:20-21}}), while the author of {{Psalm 88|Ps 88}} directly attributes his horrible suffering and loneliness to God (see especially vv. {{Isaiah 63:6|6-8}}, {{Isaiah 63:16|16-18}}). Both individuals make little, if any, room for intermediate causes or the principle of sin and death which ravages the human race. In the same way, the speaker in {{Isaiah 63:17|Isa 63:17}} (who evidences great spiritual sensitivity and is anything but “hardened”) may be referring to the hardships of exile, which discouraged and even embittered the people, causing many of them to retreat from their Yahwistic faith. In this case, the “hardening” in view is more indirect and can be lifted by the Lord’s intervention. Whether the hardening here is indirect or direct, it is important to recognize that the speaker sees it as one of the effects of rebellion against the Lord (note especially {{Isaiah 64:5|64:5-6}}).

*Translator's note:* Or “holy” (ASV, NASB, NRSV, TEV, NLT).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for a short time they had a possession, the people of your holiness.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “your adversaries trampled on.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “we were from antiquity” (see v. {{Isaiah 63:16|16}}). The collocation of הָיָה, מִן, and עוֹלָם (hayah, min, and ʿolam) occurs only here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you did not rule them; your name was not called over them.” The expression “the name is called over” indicates ownership; see the note at {{Isaiah 4:1|4:1}}. As these two lines stand, they are very difficult to interpret. They appear to be stating that the adversaries just mentioned in v. {{Isaiah 63:18|18}} have not been subject to the Lord’s rule in the past, perhaps explaining why they could commit the atrocity described in v. {{Isaiah 63:18|18b}}.

*Study note:* In *BHS* the chapter division occurs in a different place from the English Bible: 64:1 ET (63:19b HT) and 64:2-12 (64:1-11 HT). Beginning with 65:1 the verse numbers in the English Bible and the Hebrew Bible are again the same.

*Translator's note:* Or “the heavens.” The Hebrew term שָׁמַיִם (shamayim) may be translated “heavens” or “sky” depending on the context.

*Translator's note:* Or “quake.” נָזֹלּוּ (nazollu) is from the verbal root זָלַל (zalal, “quake”; see HALOT 272 s.v. II זלל). Perhaps there is a verbal allusion to {{Judges 5:5|Judg 5:5}}, the only other passage where this verb occurs. In that passage the poet tells how the Lord’s appearance to do battle caused the mountains to shake.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to make known your name to your adversaries.” Perhaps the infinitive construct with preposition לְ (lamed) should be construed with “come down” in v. {{Isaiah 64:1|1a}}, or subordinated to the following line: “To make known your name to your adversaries, let the nations shake from before you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[for which] we were not waiting.”

*Translator's note:* See the note at v. {{Isaiah 64:1|1}}.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from ancient times they have not heard, they have not listened.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “meet [with kindness].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the one who rejoices and does righteousness.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in your ways they remember you.”

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text reads literally, “look, you were angry, and we sinned against them continually [or perhaps, “in ancient times”] and we were delivered.” The statement makes little sense as it stands. The first vav [ו] consecutive (“and we sinned”) must introduce an explanatory clause here (see {{Numbers 1:48|Num 1:48}} and {{Isaiah 39:1|Isa 39:1}} for other examples of this relatively rare use of the vav [ו] consecutive). The final verb (if rendered positively) makes no sense in this context—God’s anger at their sin resulted in judgment, not deliverance. One of the alternatives involves an emendation to וַנִּרְשָׁע (vannirshaʿ, “and we were evil”; LXX, NRSV, TEV). The Vulgate and the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa support the MT reading. One can either accept an emendation or cast the statement as a question (as above).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and like a garment of menstruation [are] all our righteous acts”; KJV, NIV “filthy rags”; ASV “a polluted garment.”

*Translator's note:* Or “calls out in”; NASB, NIV, NRSV “calls on.”

*Translator's note:* Or “rouses himself”; NASB “arouses himself.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for you have hidden your face from us.”

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text reads literally, “and you caused us to melt in the hand of our sin.” The verb וַתְּמוּגֵנוּ (vattemugenu) is a Qal preterite second person masculine singular with a first person common plural suffix from the root מוּג (mug, “melt”). However, elsewhere the Qal of this verb is intransitive. If the verbal root מוּג (mug) is retained here, the form should be emended to a Polel pattern (וַתְּמֹגְגֵנוּ, vattemogegenu). The translation assumes an emendation to וַתְּמַגְּנֵנוּ (vattemaggenenu, “and you handed us over”). This form is a Piel preterite second person masculine singular with a first person common plural suffix from the verb מָגָן (magan, “hand over, surrender”; see *HALOT* 545 s.v. מגן and BDB 171 s.v. מָגָן). The point is that God has abandoned them to their sinful ways and no longer seeks reconciliation.

*Translator's note:* On the force of וְעַתָּה (veʿattah) here, see *HALOT* 902 s.v. עַתָּה.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the work of your hand.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not remember sin continually.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Look, gaze at your people, all of us.” Another option is to translate, “Take a good look! We are all your people.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “holy” (so KJV, NASB, NRSV, NLT); NIV “sacred.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “our source of pride.”

*Translator's note:* Or “all that we valued has become a ruin.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “because of these”; KJV, ASV “for these things.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I allowed myself to be sought by those who did not ask.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I allowed myself to be found by those who did not seek.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “call out in”; NASB, NIV, NRSV “call on.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who walked [in] the way that is not good, after their thoughts.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the people who provoke me to anger to my face continually.”

*Translator's note:* Or “gardens” (KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps, “on tiles.”

*Study note:* Perhaps the worship of underworld deities or dead spirits is in view.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text reads literally, “and in the watches they spend the night.” Some understand נְּצוּרִים (netsurim) as referring to “secret places” or “caves,” while others emend the text to וּבֵין צוּרִים (uven tsurim, “between the rocky cliffs”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the flesh of the pig”; KJV, NAB, NASB “swine’s flesh.”

*Text-critical note:* The marginal reading (*Qere*), supported by the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa, reads מְרַק (meraq, “broth”), while the consonantal text (*Kethib*) has פְרַק (feraq, “fragment”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Look, it is written before me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will pay back into their lap.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the iniquities of your fathers.”

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps, “taunted”; KJV “blasphemed”; NAB “disgraced”; NASB “scorned”; NIV “defied”; NRSV “reviled.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will measure out their pay [from the] beginning into their lap,” i.e., he will give them everything they have earned.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “just as.” In the Hebrew text the statement is one long sentence, “Just as…, so I will do….”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for a blessing is in it.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “by not destroying everyone.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it.” The third feminine singular pronominal suffix probably refers to the land that contains the aforementioned mountains.

*Study note:* Sharon was a plain located to the west, along the Mediterranean coast north of Joppa and south of Carmel.

*Study note:* The *Valley of Achor* (“Achor” means “trouble” in Hebrew) was the site of Achan’s execution. It was located to the east, near Jericho.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a resting place for cattle”; NASB, NIV “for herds.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for my people who seek me.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has simply, “forget.” The words “about worshiping at” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew has לַגַּד (laggad, “for Gad”), the name of a pagan deity. See *HALOT* 176 s.v. II גַּד 2.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew has לַמְנִי (lamni, “for Meni”), the name of a pagan deity. See *HALOT* 602 s.v. מְגִי.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I assign you to the sword.” Some emend the Qal verb form מָנִיתִי (maniti, “I assign”) to the Piel מִנִּיתִי (minniti, “ I ordain”). The verb sounds like the name of the god Meni (מְנִי, meni, “Destiny, Fate”). The sound play draws attention to the irony of the statement. The sinners among God’s people worship the god Meni, apparently in an effort to ensure a bright destiny for themselves. But the Lord is the one who really determines their destiny and he has decreed their demise.

*Translator's note:* Or “at the slaughter”; NIV11 “in the slaughter”; NLT “before the executioner.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “that which is evil in my eyes.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the good of the heart.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the pain of the heart.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the breaking of the spirit.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you will leave your name for an oath to my chosen ones.”

*Study note:* For an example of such a curse formula see Jer 29:22.

*Translator's note:* Or “in the land” (NIV, NCV, NRSV). The same phrase occurs again later in this verse, with the same options.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will pronounce a blessing by the God of truth.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will take an oath by the God of truth.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for the former distresses will be forgotten, and they will be hidden from my eyes.”

The point would be that even in this new era the snake (often taken as a symbol of Satan) remains under God’s curse. However, it is unlikely that such an allusion exists. Even if there is an echo of {{Genesis 3:14|Gen 3:14}}, the primary allusion is to {{Isaiah 11:8|11:8}}, where snakes are pictured as no longer dangerous. In God’s sight the one who sacrifices is like (i.e., regarded as) a murderer or one whose worship is ritually defiled or idolatrous. The translation above assumes that the language is not metaphorical, but descriptive of the sinners’ hypocritical behavior. (Note the last two lines of the verse, which suggest they are guilty of abominable practices.) On the one hand, they act pious and offer sacrifices, but at the same time they commit violent crimes against men, defile their sacrifices, and worship other gods.

*Study note:* The significance of breaking a dog’s neck is uncertain, though the structure of the statement when compared to the preceding and following lines suggests the action is viewed in a negative light. According to {{Exodus 13:13|Exod 13:13}} and {{Exodus 34:20|34:20}}, one was to “redeem” a firstborn donkey by offering a lamb; if one did not “redeem” the firstborn donkey in this way, then its neck must be broken. According to {{Deuteronomy 21:1|Deut 21:1-9}} a heifer’s neck was to be broken as part of the atonement ritual to purify the land from the guilt of bloodshed. It is not certain if these passages relate in any way to the action described in {{Isaiah 66:3|Isa 66:3}}.

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text reads literally “and I, their deeds and their thoughts, am coming.” The syntax here is very problematic, suggesting that the text may need emendation. Some suggest that the words “their deeds and their thoughts” have been displaced from v. {{Isaiah 66:17|17}}. This line presents two primary challenges. In the first place, the personal pronoun “I” has no verb after it. Most translations insert “know” for the sake of clarity (NASB, NRSV, NLT, ESV). The NIV11 has “I, because of what they have planned and done…” Since God’s “knowledge” of Israel’s sin occasions judgment, the verb “hate” is an option as well (see above translation). The feminine form of the next verb (בָּאָה, baʾah) could be understood in one of two ways. One could provide an implied noun “time” (עֵת, ʿet) and render the next line “the time is coming/has come” (NASB, ESV). One could also emend the feminine verb to the masculine בָּא (baʾ) and have the “I” at the beginning of the line govern this verb as well (for the Lord is speaking here): “I am coming” (cf. NIV, NCV, NRSV, TEV, NLT).
